reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: Primary (effort) thrombosis of the axillary-subclavian vein, representing the venous form of thoracic outlet syndrome.
Typically affects young, healthy, muscular individuals after repetitive or strenuous upper-limb activity such as throwing, weightlifting or swimming, usually in the dominant arm.
Presents with sudden arm swelling, heaviness, cyanotic discolouration and dilated superficial collateral veins over the shoulder and chest wall.

The underlying cause is venous compression within the costoclavicular space by the first rib, the subclavius and anterior scalene muscles and the costoclavicular ligament, with repetitive endothelial trauma and thrombosis.
Duplex ultrasound is first-line; contrast, CT or MR venography with the arm in provocative positions confirms extrinsic compression.
Contemporary management combines early catheter-directed thrombolysis with first-rib resection and thoracic outlet decompression to address the anatomical cause.
It must be distinguished from secondary upper-limb deep vein thrombosis related to central venous catheters or malignancy, which is more common overall.
A thrombophilia screen may be considered in selected patients, but the primary abnormality is mechanical.
reference.pathophysiology: Repetitive hyperabduction and extension of the arm compress the subclavian vein as it passes through the narrow costoclavicular space, bounded by the first rib, clavicle, subclavius muscle, costoclavicular ligament and anterior scalene. Chronic mechanical trauma produces intimal hyperplasia, perivenous fibrosis and venous wall injury which, combined with stasis during compression, triggers thrombosis by completing Virchow's triad. The dominant arm is usually affected because of greater muscular hypertrophy and activity. Untreated, residual stenosis and fibrosis perpetuate obstruction, driving collateral formation and post-thrombotic symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary upper-limb deep vein thrombosis from a central venous catheter, pacemaker or malignancy
Muscle strain or rotator cuff injury
Neurogenic or arterial thoracic outlet syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound of the upper-limb veins
Contrast venography, often as a prelude to thrombolysis
CT or MR venography with provocative arm positioning
Chest and thoracic outlet imaging for a cervical rib or bony anomaly
Assessment for occult malignancy when features suggest secondary thrombosis
Dynamic positional imaging to demonstrate extrinsic compression after clot clearance
redFlags: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens with massive swelling, cyanosis and threatened limb viability.
Signs of pulmonary embolism, which can complicate upper-limb deep vein thrombosis.
Rapidly progressive swelling with neurological or arterial compromise.
Features suggesting an underlying malignancy in apparent secondary thrombosis.
Failure to improve or early re-thrombosis after anticoagulation.
reference.prognosis: With prompt thrombolysis and thoracic outlet decompression most young patients regain a patent vein and return to full activity, whereas delayed or anticoagulation-only treatment leaves a significant minority with post-thrombotic arm symptoms and activity limitation.
pitfalls: Treating with anticoagulation alone and ignoring the underlying mechanical compression, leading to recurrence and post-thrombotic morbidity.
Delaying venography and thrombolysis beyond the window when the clot is still amenable.
Failing to image in provocative positions and thereby missing dynamic compression once the vein is recanalised.
Mislabelling effort thrombosis as a simple muscle strain in an athlete.
Overlooking a cervical rib or other bony anomaly on the affected side.
